extracted.intended_audience: Korean policymakers and regulators, SMBA and RRC staff, SME associations and regulatory reform practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural standards for SME-focused regulatory reform in Korea, including mandatory RIA on SMEs, institutional roles (RRC, SMBA, SMEs Ombudsman), alternatives to regulation, stakeholder engagement, and appeals. Targeted at officials and organisations designing, reviewing or reforming regulations that affect SMEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry classification source
rubrics_metrics.description: Industry classification and industry codes in this table are derived from Korea Standard Industrial Classification (KSIC) in accordance with Article 22 of the Statistics Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note and source: Article 2 of Framework Act on SMEs and Article 8 of Enforcement Decree of the Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory RIA on SMEs
rubrics_metrics.description: If any central administrative agency introduces a new regulation or strengthens an existing regulation that has a potential impact on SMEs, regulatory impact assessment on SMEs must be conducted accordingly, and its statement must be made public during the advance notice period of the proposed legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A RIAS on SMEs is made public on the concerned central administrative agency’s website, the Regulatory Information Portal, and the Foreign Investment Portal to ensure transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: RIA content requirements (analysis and mitigation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A RIAS on SMEs must include quantitative or qualitative analyses on the effects of the new or reinforced regulations on SMEs, including the cost and benefit analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RIA should mitigate regulatory burdens on SMEs by considering alternatives to the proposed regulation, prevent introduction of regulations that overlap with existing regulations, and evaluate whether the regulation is in line with global standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: RIA process and review flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory review flow: the RRO first determines if the regulation affects SMEs and, if so, transfers the task to the SMBA; the SMBA works closely with the CRIA to propose alternatives, conduct cost-benefit analysis, and gather expert opinions; the SMBA then submits the drafted RIAS on SMEs to the RRC; the RRC reviews the regulatory proposal and determines whether to approve or reject the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors and responsibilities are delineated (RRO, SMBA, CRIA, RRC); the RRC utilises submitted RIAS to review regulatory proposals and can recommend withdrawal or amendment of unreasonable proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-phase RIA on SMEs
rubrics_metrics.description: RIA on SMEs is composed of three phases: completion of RIA report, RIA on SMEs (conducting the assessment), and regulatory review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first phase (completion of RIA statement) should include: i) confirmation whether the regulation pertains to SMEs, ii) the state of the regulated businesses by size, iii) the ratio of regulatory burdens by enterprise size, iv) the outcomes of consultations with SMEs, and v) alternatives to alleviate regulatory burdens on SMEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives to regulatory proposals — Fair regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Enhancing regulatory equity by enforcing regulations tailored in accordance with firm size and capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tailoring standards, procedures, and time frames of registration requirements and document submission to firm size/capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives to regulatory proposals — Reasonable regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibiting overlapping regulations, alleviating regulatory barriers to entry, and simplifying excessively burdensome regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: consolidating overlapping certifications and land‑use regulations, reducing burden of mandatory training, and simplifying entry barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives to regulatory proposals — Selective regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting all kinds of economic activities and regulating performance and outcomes instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: performance-based regulation and negative-list approach (allow all activities except those explicitly prohibited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives to regulatory proposals — Flexible regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Flexible enforcement of regulation, depending on the economic or business situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use of sunset clauses and temporary regulatory relief; approaches such as Cost-in, Cost-out (CICO) and temporary suspension/relief to mitigate burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-track approach to reducing disproportionate burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-track approach: 1) Proportional Regulation for SMEs — where regulations can classify regulated entities by business size, apply regulatory burdens proportionally; 2) Building SME‑friendly regulatory environment — give priority to improving regulations that cause unreasonable regulatory burdens on SMEs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This institutional approach prioritises proportionality and targeted reform of regulations with excessive burdens; underpins policies like tailored regulation and prioritisation of problematic regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of the Thorn‑under‑the‑Fingernail (RTUF)
rubrics_metrics.description: RTUF aims to remove regulatory difficulties of SMEs; 'thorn‑under‑the‑fingernail regulations' are regulations that are easily neglected yet impose significant impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RTUF is an active reform tool involving SME organisations (KBIZ, SMBA, SMEs Ombudsman) to identify and reform such regulations; e.g., ~300 thorn‑under‑the‑fingernail regulations were removed in the first half of 2013.

rubrics_metrics.name: SMEs Ombudsman core functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Main functions: 1) Identifying and improving regulations pertaining to small and medium enterprises (through suggestions and recommendations); 2) Investigating, analysing, resolving, and evaluating regulatory difficulties; 3) Responding to complaints on unreasonable regulations; 4) Actively providing recommendations on administrative exemptions; and 5) Implementing inspections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Ombudsman is an independent agency established under the Framework Act on Small and Medium Enterprises and can make recommendations, support reform, and operate an Ombudsman Support Team to facilitate reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: SMEs Ombudsman legal obligations and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ombudsman’s legal obligations include providing recommendations on improvements, investigating the performance of concerned agencies, conducting stakeholder engagement, and publishing its work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Ombudsman is obligated to report to the RRC, the State Council Meeting, and the National Assembly on an annual basis to ensure accountability for its independent activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional roles and responsibilities (RRC, SMBA, PPJRAI, CRIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Roles: RRC acts as central oversight body to discuss regulatory reform direction, overhaul existing regulation, and evaluate new/strengthened regulations; PPJRAI identifies on‑site regulatory difficulties and inspects reform progress; SMBA is tasked with quality management of regulations through RIA on SMEs and holds main authority over RIA on SMEs; CRIA (Korea Small Business Institute) provides consultation in drafting RIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These roles are interlinked: SMBA conducts RIAs and submits RIAS to RRC; RRC uses RIAS to review and recommend actions to administrative agencies. PPJRAI is a public‑private joint initiative to process petitions on existing business-related regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder engagement and consultation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Close communication with businesses throughout the entire cycle of regulatory reform is a core principle. Channels include regulatory consultation centres (regional SMBA offices), Small and Medium Business Corporation (SBC), SEMAS, KICOX, regulatory petition centres, KBIZ, KCCI and industry associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sufficient consultations (open discussions, briefings, general public hearings) are required especially where conflicts of interest arise; expert panels and organisations (e.g., Korea Society for Regulatory Studies) provide non‑biased alternatives and advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority targets for SME regulatory reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary targets of reform are regulations that have significant spill‑over effects, particularly on business investment and job creation, and regulations that impose unreasonable burdens on SMEs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies and programs (e.g., tailored regulatory approach, Plan for 10% reduction of economic regulation, regulatory reduction programmes) focus on these priority areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal process and conflict resolution during reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicts of interest (between SMEs, between SMEs and large firms, or across sectors) commonly arise during reform. To resolve disputes, alternatives to the proposed regulation must be arranged after sufficient consultations with stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, rational alternative measures are arranged through discussions in the OPC and Ministerial Meetings on Regulatory Reform; expert opinions from academic and industry associations are consulted to seek rational, non‑biased alternatives.
